say: This car is flying forward. So why do its wheels sometimes look like they're spinning backwards? Your eyes aren't broken. The camera is tricking you.
A video isn't really moving. It's a stack of still photos, usually twenty four, thirty, or sixty every second, flipped so fast your brain sees motion.
When a wheel turns slowly, each photo catches the spokes a little further along. Forward, forward, forward. Easy.
Now speed it up. Between two photos, each spoke travels almost all the way to where the next spoke used to be.
Your brain compares the two photos and picks the shortest path. And the shortest path is a tiny step backwards. So the wheel seems to spin in reverse.
Hit the exact speed where every spoke lands right where another one was, and the wheel looks frozen, even at full speed. Helicopter blades do this too.
It's called the wagon wheel effect, named after old western movies where stagecoach wheels kept rolling the wrong way.
The weirdest part? Some people see it in real life too, in normal daylight, and scientists still argue about exactly why.
